An Optimization Approach to Automatic
Construction of Browsable Concept Index for
Organizing Online Educational Content
1st Assma Boughoula
Univ. of IL Urbana-Champaign
boughou1@illinois.edu
2nd Kevin Ros
Univ. of IL Urbana-Champaign
kjros2@illinois.edu
3rd ChengXiang Zhai
Univ. of IL Urbana-Champaign
czhai@illinois.edu
Abstract—As learning becomes more dependent on online
learning platforms, new challenges emerge. One major challenge
is efﬁcient access to educational content as most content is
unstructured and scattered on the Web. Indeed, there is a
great need for organizing educational content and presenting
it in a semantically structured and browsable format that does
not require the users’ prior knowledge of relevant content.
In this paper, we address this need by introducing a novel
semantic structure, called Browsable Concept Index (BCI), to
bring semantic structures to educational content. A BCI consists
of a set of representative concepts that form a graph with each
(weighted) edge indicating strength of association between two
concepts and each concept node being linked to the text segments
in the collection of documents that cover the concept. The
BCI effectively integrates scattered textual content and enables
efﬁcient access to the content by users in multiple ways including:
semantic browsing, exploratory and targeted information seeking,
and collaborative information seeking. We further propose an
optimization-based algorithm to automatically create a BCI based
on a collection of educational textual content. Experiments on
Coursera course content demonstrate that the our algorithm is
effective, allowing the automatic construction of a useful BCI
that can facilitate online learning.
Index Terms—browsable concept index, concept graph, seman-
tic integration of content, online educational content, semantic
browsing

One major challenge is efficient access to educational content as most content is unstructured and scattered on the Web. Indeed, there is a great need for organizing educational content and presenting it in a semantically structured and browsable format that does not require the users’ prior knowledge of relevant content. In this paper, we address this need by introducing a novel semantic structure, called Browsable Concept Index (BCI), to bring semantic structures to educational content. I NTRODUCTION Online educational content and online learning platforms have revolutionized education around the world. We have come to depend on online resources (in video and text forms) to aid our learning, and we are continuing to move away from traditional forms such as physical reference textbooks and handwritten notes. The type of learning (and learners) nowadays has changed too: in the recent past, the vast majority of learners were traditional students, following curricula designed by profes- sional instructors and advisors in an academic institutional setting. But recently, we have seen an unprecedented rise in the number of “independent learners” who do not follow a structured curriculum but are rather ad-hoc learners targeting specific new concepts and skills to learn. This is especially true of Computer Science education since the field continues to grow very rapidly, and hence learners are finding them- selves coming back to learn new material well past the time they earned their degrees. “Continuing education” scenarios such as this are becoming the norm across many disciplines. Thus, independent, ad-hoc learners are quickly becoming the most important user group for emerging online educational technologies and platforms on the Web. This new shift presents a new set of challenges for learners, instructors, and content providers. One challenge from the learners’ point of view is ease of access: how can learners identify their target learning material without having access to one-on-one expert guidance from instructors and advisors? Currently the main tools available for such learners are general Web search engines such as Google and search en- gines provided by specific platforms such as Coursera and edX. However, independent learners have to guide their own learning journey but generally do not have the prior knowledge that would help them identify useful query terms. In addition to this, the ad-hoc approach to learning means that learners are not searching for whole courses and sitting through all the modules in chronological order. Instead, they need to pick the segments of material to go through in order to meet their target learning goal. The challenges discussed here demonstrate a need to pre

sections.text: O PTIMIZATION In this section, we discuss the optimization criteria for building a BCI and explicitly define the objective function. A. Optimization Criteria Our goal in constructing a BCI is to have users look at the final selected concepts as a snapshot “concept summary” of the content in the collection D as well as use the reference mapping G to easily navigate to relevant text segments in D . The text segments in the mapping G for a selected concept should provide a snapshot of what the concept is about according to content in D . With this in mind, we propose the following optimization criteria:

sections.heading: Relevance
sections.text: : a concept entry G [ c i ] in G should map to text segments where the concept is central to the discussion. Segments where the concept is mentioned in passing and is not central to discussion should not be included in the concept entry in G . 2)

sections.heading: Completeness
sections.text: : all relevant text segments should be included in the mapping of the concept entry G [ c i ] . This is important because providing a complete “snapshot summary” of concepts increases the utility of the BCI as a reference for users. 3)

sections.heading: Global Coverage
sections.text: : the content in the entire document collection D should be reasonably uniformly covered by entry mappings in the BCI (i.e. we should not see long stretches of content that no concept entry refers to). This criterion helps us make sure we provide a complete set of concepts discussed in the content. If there are, however, long stretches of content that no entry in the BCI refers to, then that would indicate that either we have not met our completeness criteria for G and some entries are missing relevant sections of material, or that we have not met our recall criteria for S and some central concepts were not selected. B. Objective Function Design Here we present our designed objective function and explain how it optimizes the criteria in III-A. The proposed objective function is composed of two main parts with the use of em- bedding vectors [9], [10] to represent concepts and reference text segments. 1)

sections.heading: Cluster quality measure:
sections.text: Using embedding vectors to represent each reference text t k , and looking at G as a set of labeled clusters G [ c i ] where the labels are the concepts c i , we measure the quality of G ’s overall reference mapping using the Calinski-Harabasz index [11] for clusters. We use the Calinski-Harabasz index because it measures both within-cluster compactness as well as between-cluster dispersion. The higher the CH index score, the better the clustering quality. Measuring the within-cluster compactness ensures that we are con- sidering the relevance criteria for G (by ensuring that all segments are closely relevant to the ’label’ concept) and the prominance criteria for S (by ensuring that con- cepts with reference segments that are too scattered are discouraged). Measuring the between-cluster dispersion ensures that we are considering the uniqueness criteria for S (by ensuring that the semantic difference between concepts is maximized, thus discouraging redundant concepts). Since the CH index can have values [0 , + ∞ ) , and since we prefer cluster quality to have range [0 , 1] we rewrite cluster quality as: ClusterQuality ( G ) := 1 − 1 CH ( G ) where CH ( G ) is the Calinski-Harabasz index score of G . 2)

sections.heading: Global coverage measure:
sections.text: This measures the percent- age of content covered by the index mapping G , and is calculated as the total length of all uncovered text content divided by the total length of all the documents in D , subtracted from 1 to ensure its in the range [0 , 1] . Maximizing the global coverage measure ensures that we are considering the recall criteria for S (if we miss a central concept, this measure suffers), the completeness criteria for G (if we omit to include all relevant segments in the mapping for a concept, this measure suffers), and the global coverage criteria for G . GlobalCoverage ( S, G ) := 1 − | uncovered | L where | uncovered | is the total length of uncovered segments and L is the total length of all content. OBJ ( S, G ) = ( ClusterQuality ( G ) + GlobalCoverage ( S, G )) / 2 = [(1 − 1 CH ( G ) ) + (1 −| uncovered | L )] / 2 (1) By averaging the two components of the objective function (equation (1) above), we ensure that the objective function’s values are always in the range of [0 , 1] . sections.heading: Select-Map-Connect
sections.text: (SMC) algorithm: it iteratively updates the variables S (update selected concepts), G (update the mapping of the selected concepts to text segments in D ), and A (recalculating the semantic similarity or connections between pairs of selected concepts). The updates follow a set of heuristics designed to improve the optimization criteria in III-A. We discuss the design of the heuristic conditions below. A. Select-Map-Connect

sections.heading: Text representation:
sections.text: Embedding vectors are used to repre- sent text data such as the text segments referenced by entries in the mapping G , or candidate concepts in C . We can use any embedding methods; in our implementation we use pre-trained BERT embeddings [9].

sections.heading: Drop:
sections.text: For each concept’s mapped segments in G , drop any outlier segments to improve the segments’ cluster quality. This improves the relevance criteria in opti- mizing G . Intuitively, we expect a central concept to have a clearly defined cluster of mentions in a span of proximate content. This clear cluster indicates where the concept was a central topic of discussion in D . Any other scattered mentions of the concept (i.e., “outliers”) would not be included in the concept’s G mapping. The “outliers” are determined by calculating the Z - scores for each mapped text segment’s embedding vector and dropping those with Z - scores higher than 3 . 0 , meaning they deviate more than 3 standard deviations from the mean and are typically considered outliers. •

sections.text: For each mapped segment ( t k , loc t k ) in G [ c i ] , expand t k by including the sentence before loc t k , the sentence after , or both sentences. Intu- itively, the completeness criteria for G is improved by including all relevant sentences discussing the concept. And since we expect a concept’s discussion to often span multiple consecutive sentences in the material, expanding by including neighboring sentences first makes sense. The compactness measure is expected to keep improving when adding neighboring sentences if these sentences are discussing the same topic and thus share a semantic context. As soon as a neighboring sentence starts dis- cussing a different concept signaling a topic shift, the embedding vector for that sentence will reflect this shift, and we expect the compactness measure to be similarly affected as well. By expanding in this way, we expect to identify the boundaries of a concept’s mapped reference segments correctly i.e. including all sentences that discuss the concept, but stopping just shy of sentences signaling a change in the topic of discussion. •

sections.text: This step’s goal is to improve the relevance cri- teria for optimizing G through reducing overlap between mapped segments of different concepts by shrinking over- lapping segments until they no longer share intersecting text. Thus it should not be included in the mapped reference segments of selected concepts.

sections.text: Drop a concept from the selected set if its mapped reference segments are completely covered by other con- cepts’ mapped reference segments. If this condition is true, then this indicates that the concept is not a central concept in D . We expect that deselecting such concepts will improve the prominance criteria for S . •

sections.text: If the calculated similarity score A [ i ][ j ] between two selected concepts c i and c j exceeds a threshold value B high , then c i and c j are considered to be duplicate concepts and must be merged. The dominant concept (i.e. the one with more reference segments) should be retained while the other is deselected and its mapped reference segments are added to the dominant concept’s entry in G . We choose to retain the concept with more references since presumably its specific phrasing is more commonly used and understood. •

Intuitively, if we keep adding the candidates that add the most previously uncovered content to the index mapping in each iteration, then we will improve the global coverage of the BCI.

Note that for consistency, we ran this random experiment 10 times for each MOOC dataset. We can see from the table that for both MOOC datasets, the final resulting BCI from our algorithm scores significantly better than a random BCI. sections.heading: Specific techniques for designing retrieval functions:
sections.text: We see several important techniques covered in this MOOC about how to design a retrieval function, including, e.g., “learning to rank”, and “query likelihood”, which are both commonly used techniques in research papers. Since our heuristics do not include any linguistic knowledge, these results show that the algorithm effectively picks up closely related concepts due to the effectiveness of embedding representation in capturing word semantics. These complementary neighbors enable a learner to flexibly explore different learning paths depending on their interests or needs. Once a learner navigates into a related neighboring concept, they can see the neighbors of the new concept, thus enabling a learner to explore a learning path based on their interests. Such a path can be viewed as a natural way to formulate a query (i.e., all the concepts along a path can be combined into a query) to enable a retrieval system to accurately locate the most relevant educational content for the learner to interact with. This query construction process is especially useful for users who do not have sufficient background knowledge to effectively formulate a query, which is often the case when a learner explores an unfamiliar topic. Figure 4 shows an example of a learning path. A learner can start at the concept ”retrieval function”, navigate to ”learning to rank” which refers to the topic of optimizing retrieval functions, from there the learner can jump to ”recommender systems” which is a very popular application area for text retrieval. Interestingly, this specific path reflects the preferred order of learning these concepts in most instructor designed modules in text retrieval. 2)

R ELATED W ORK Much work has been done on extracting data from educa- tional content (e.g., automatic annotation system [12], concept hierarchy construction [13], concept dependency graph con- struction [14], and concept extraction from MOOC [15]). Our work is complementary to these previous studies and can be combined with them; e.g. using the methods in those previous studies to post-process the constructed BCI or using them to improve the construction of the initial set of candidate terms in our work. Regarding index construction, Csomai and Mihalcea ex- plored various unsupervised methods to create back-of-the- book indices [16]. From experiments using 29 books, they find that combining multiple term extraction methods and ranking heuristics result in the best performance. In a similar fashion, Csomai and Mihalcea also proposed a combination of features to generate back-of-the-book indices in a supervised manner [17]. Wu et al. also attempted to automatically construct back- of-the-book indices using both the structural information of the books as well as external term knowledge from databases such as Wikipedia [18]. Text mining techniques, such as Automatic Keyword Extraction, have also been used to generate back- of-the-book indices, as described in Koutropoulou and Gal- lopoulos [19]. All such methods can be used for supplying potentially better initial candidate terms to our algorithm. Compared with many index construction methods, a main distinguishing factor of our proposed BCI approach is its efficiency and scalability. The construction of the BCI is unsupervised and is therefore not limited by training data or to a specific domain. Moreover, the BCI can be applied to any course on major online learning platforms as long as the lecture transcripts are available (which are generally easy to obtain from lecture videos by using speech recognition). Additionally, since the BCI uniquely includes connections between concepts, it can be used by learners as a tool for guided exploration of educational material. More importantly, our work is innovative in that BCI is constructed based on a set of well-defined optimization criteria with simultaneous optimization of both the selection of terms and the mapping of terms to text segments. Our problem formulation is also more challenging than book index construction because we model dependency among the selected concepts whereas the existing work often frames the problem with simplification assumptions such as treating each index term independently.

sections.text: F UTURE W ORK In this paper, we proposed a novel idea of automatically con- structing a Browsable Concept Index (BCI) to bring semantic structures to scattered online educational content to facilitate online learning. We addressed the problem by defining the concept of a BCI and proposing an optimization algorithm for constructing a BCI. We proposed multiple desirable objectives and formally framed the problem of BCI construction as an optimization problem where concept selection and mapping of concept to text segments are simultaneously optimized. We proposed a heuristic Select-Map-Connection algorithm to solve the optimization problem and automatically create a BCI based on text descriptions of educational content. Experiments on Coursera MOOC content demonstrate that our algorithm is effective and scalable. A BCI effectively integrates scattered text content and enables users easier and more efficient access to the content 30 Authorized licensed use limited to: University of Lancashire. Although we focused on studying BCI construction in the education domain, the proposed algorithm is general and can be used to construct a BCI to organize other kind of online textual content.
